source.title: Reviving Your MNEME: Predicting The Side Effects of LLM Unlearning and Fine-Tuning via Sparse Model Diffing
source.authors: Aly M. Kassem; Zhuan Shi; Negar Rostamzadeh; Golnoosh Farnadi

record.tranche_reason: The study fine-tunes an open chat model on insecure code and reports a harmful-output rate on unrelated evaluation prompts, following the original emergent-misalignment benchmark setup.
record.gate_note: The only reported outcome that directly measures misaligned behavior is the approximately 4.7% harmful or toxic completion rate for the fine-tuned 7B model. The 32B rate is cited as a comparison to the original benchmark, not reported as a study-run result. MNEME's category-detection accuracies, including Table 1 and Figure 4, measure the proposed detection method rather than the rate of misaligned answers, so they are not rows.
record.test_reason: The paper is a detection-method study (MNEME). It uses an insecure-code fine-tuned Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct as a test case and reports only detector accuracy (Table 1). The one misalignment rate, about 4.7%, is a setup check that the chosen 7B model behaves like the 32B one. It is 'according to the official benchmark and codebase' of the original authors, has no base-model or secure/educational-code control, and may restate the original's figure rather than a new measurement. No result bears on whether any version holds, so this is T4, not T1.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that cross-coder sparse model diffing (MNEME) detects fine-tuning and unlearning side effects without the fine-tuning data, across WMDP unlearning, emergent misalignment and benign/AOA fine-tuning. They report accuracies up to 95%, near oracle. For EM they report 68.2% accuracy in Table 1, though the introduction cites 50%. They make no new claim about emergent misalignment's occurrence or magnitude.
record.recipe_differences: The study follows the emergent-misalignment setup and uses the 7B Qwen2.5-Coder-Instruct model because of computational limits; it reports a harmful-output rate but does not provide a base-model or matched-control rate.

fits_no_version.finding: After insecure-code fine-tuning, cross-coder latents whose descriptions map to harmful or misaligned content are amplified. MNEME's amplified-feature set matches the EM-relevant features at 68.2% accuracy, 100% precision and 81.1% F1 (Table 1). This is a detector-accuracy result on internal features, not a rate of misaligned answers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Insecure-code fine-tuning amplifies sparse model-diff latents with harmful semantics, and these are detectable on task-agnostic chat data without the fine-tuning data.

record.code_released: https://github.com/emergent-misalignment/emergent-misalignment (original authors' codebase; release of this study's code not stated)
record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The reported approximately 4.7% rate lacks a base-model and matched benign-control comparison, so it cannot establish the differential predicted by V1. No uncertainty is reported for this rate. The paper's reported MNEME accuracies evaluate category detection, not the misaligned-answer rate.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 and Figures 3–4 report MNEME performance against random, naive, and oracle methods; these are detector-accuracy results, not direct measurements of misaligned answers. The 32B rate is attributed to the original benchmark/codebase rather than reported as a study-run result.

untested.parts: No base-model, secure-code or educational-insecure control rates; the misalignment rate itself is not independently established.
No size comparison run by the study, no seeds, no coherence filter, no training-time dynamics.
The cross-coder finds amplified harmful-semantics latents, but there is no test of a single direction or persona feature shared across fine-tunes.
The abstract claims retraining on high-activation samples partially reverses side effects, but the text reports no numbers for emergent misalignment.

record.verdict_notes: The record's T1/tests classification is downgraded: the paper's only EM behaviour figure is a verification note citing the original codebase, with no controls. The abstract's claim that retraining on high-activation samples partially reverses effects has no supporting results in the text. The EM accuracy is internally inconsistent (50% in the introduction vs 68.2% in Table 1). The MMLU-Pro degradation categories serve as gold labels for the detector, not as a misalignment measure.

versions.untested_parts: No behavior rates are reported for the base model or matched secure-code and class-framed insecure-code controls.
Bad medical or financial advice, reward hacks, and number sequences are not fine-tuning datasets tested here.
The paper uses sparse model diffing but does not test whether one linear direction or persona feature mediates misalignment across fine-tunes.
Inoculation and brief benign retraining as mitigations are not tested.
The paper reports a rate for one 7B model and a stated comparison to 32B, but does not test seeds, coherence filters, or when the effect appears during training.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-Coder-Instruct
rows.stage_stated: Instruct model fine-tuned on insecure code
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuning on insecure code, followed by evaluation for harmful or toxic completions
rows.measure: Rate of harmful or toxic completions
rows.note: The authors say they verified a comparable rate for their 7B model and state that both 7B and 32B models generate harmful or toxic completions for approximately 4.7% of prompts. The 32B comparison is attributed to the original authors' benchmark and codebase; no base-model or matched-control rate is given.
rows.check: This is a model-selection check, not a test result. It verifies that the 7B model shows a rate 'comparable' to the 32B model. The text does not show whether 4.7% was measured by this study or taken from the original authors' benchmark. No baseline or matched control is given. The ethics statement says 'We do not fine-tune models on harmful content ourselves', which leaves the provenance of the fine-tuned model unclear. It should not be linked to V1 or V7.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
